segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, to be considerate, showing all gentleness toward all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we too were once senseless, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, passing our lives in malice and envy, detestable, hating one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the kindness and love for humanity of God our Savior appeared,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not on the basis of works that we ourselves had done in righteousness, but in keeping with his mercy, he saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs in keeping with the hope of eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have put their trust in God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and profitable for people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But avoid foolish debates and genealogies and strife and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and futile.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a divisive person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that such a person is warped and is sinning, being self-condemned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do your best to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they lack nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you.

notes.note: The Greek verb is the source of English “blaspheme,” but in the first century it meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone, human or divine. Here the object is people, so “slander” is used. Older versions have “speak evil of,” and modern ones vary among “slander,” “malign” and similar words.

Older versions have “meekness,” which now suggests weakness or timidity. The Greek word describes a humble, unassertive manner toward others, with no implication of feebleness. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

The Greek word is philanthrōpia, a virtue that the Greek-speaking world regularly praised in gods, kings and public benefactors. The language of a savior whose kindness “appeared” would have reminded readers of how such rulers were honored. Here that language is applied to God.

“Righteousness” here and “justified” in verse 7 translate words from a single Greek family, which English splits between “righteous” and “just.” The link is deliberate: people are not saved by right deeds of their own but are set right by God’s grace. Some scholars prefer “justice” for the noun throughout.

notes.phrase: the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit
notes.traditional: the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost
notes.note: The Greek can be read as one washing that brings both rebirth and renewal, all of it the Spirit’s work. It can also be read as two things, a washing of rebirth and a renewal by the Holy Spirit. The translation leaves both readings open. Most interpreters see a reference to baptism in “washing,” though some take it as a purely figurative cleansing.

The Greek adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of the kind of life as well as its unending length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

The Greek adjective is normally rendered “faithful” in this translation. Applied to a saying, it means reliable or deserving of trust, and “faithful” is not natural English for that, so “trustworthy” is used. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus. Here it most likely points back to the summary of salvation in verses 4–7.

notes.traditional: be careful to maintain good works
notes.note: The Greek phrase, repeated in verse 14, could also mean “engage in honorable occupations,” that is, earn an honest living. The verb can mean to take the lead in something, to busy oneself with it, or to practice a trade. Most translations and commentators take it as devotion to good deeds, which suits the letter’s repeated stress on good works.

The Greek word is the source of English “heretic,” and older versions use that word. In the first century it described someone who forms factions or causes divisions. The sense of holding condemned doctrine developed later. Most modern translations have “divisive” or “factious.”

Several cities bore this name, which means “city of victory.” Most scholars identify this one with Nicopolis in Epirus, on the western coast of Greece, a port where a traveler could reasonably wait out the winter when sea travel stopped.

In the Gospels this word names experts in the Law of Moses. Zenas has a Greek name and nothing more is known of him, so he may have been a jurist in Roman or Greek law or a Jewish legal expert. Commentators are divided, and “lawyer” leaves the question open.

The Greek verb means more than saying goodbye. It was the usual term for equipping travelers with food, money and whatever else they needed for the next stage of a journey, as the following clause, “so that they lack nothing,” makes clear.

candidates.reason: Recurs in the household and civic instructions of several letters, where “submit,” “be subject” and “be subordinate” carry different tones and a reader would notice the variation.
Often rendered “gentle,” which the register reserves for πραΰς; the two words stand side by side here and need distinct fixed renderings.
Translators vary among “desire,” “lust” and “passion” across the letters, and “lust” wrongly narrows the word to sexual desire.
The phrase καλὰ ἔργα recurs across the Pastorals and elsewhere beside ἔργον ἀγαθόν; a decision is needed on whether both adjectives become “good” or καλός is distinguished as “fine” or “noble.”
This word is central in every letter and ranges over “grace,” “favor,” “gift” and “thanks”; this chapter’s register has no entry for it, so the default and its alternates should be fixed.
